validity.recommendation: no action on existence/classification — exceptionally well documented, real, operating, correctly classified interstate gas pipeline
validity.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE and CLASSIFICATION are about as strongly confirmed as this cohort gets. Pulled the actual FERC certificate order (not just news about it): 166 FERC ¶ 61,144, Docket Nos. CP15-550-000/CP15-551-000/-001, 'Venture Global Calcasieu Pass, LLC / TransCameron Pipeline, LLC', issued Feb. 21, 2019, downloaded and read with pdftotext -layout (ferc.gov/sites/default/files/CalendarFiles/20190221194809-CP15-550-000a.pdf). It grants TransCameron Pipeline, LLC authorization under NGA §7 to 'construct and operate a new interstate natural gas pipeline' — this is a FERC-jurisdictional interstate transmission line, correctly classified Fuel=Gas, not a gathering/process line. Independently corroborated by: PR Newswire release (Sept. 8, 2015, the original joint FERC application announcement, naming 'Venture Global Calcasieu Pass, LLC and TransCameron Pipeline, LLC'); an archived TransmissionHub/TD World article (Jun. 28, 2016, on the amendment dropping the West Lateral); World Oil (Feb. 22, 2019, construction-approval announcement); Oil & Gas Journal (Aug. 21, 2019, FID article, and Apr. 9, 2021, start-of-service article); Natural Gas Intelligence (Apr. 7, 2021, FERC clears pipeline for service); EIA's own Today in Energy article (2022, government source, describing the operating Calcasieu Pass terminal receiving feedgas via 'Venture Global's 24-mile, 42-inch diameter TransCameron Pipeline'); and Venture Global's own current live site (ventureglobal.com/calcasieu-pass/transcameron-pipeline/, updated Nov. 2025). These are genuinely independent origins (a federal regulator's order, a wire-service release, three separate trade-press outlets, and the operator) all describing the same physical 23.4-24-mile, 42-inch pipeline from interconnects near Grand Chenier Station to the Calcasieu Pass LNG terminal, both in Cameron Parish, LA, entering service April 2021. Not a phantom, not GEM-only — GEM's own citation pool (10 harvested references) pointed straight at this evidence and every one of the 8 live/working citations independently corroborates the row (opened all 10 harvested citations; 2 were dead — see spec note below — and recovered via Wayback / a live-site path). One caveat only: see the Capacity spec finding below.

DUPLICATE check against the 50-pipeline roster: no other row plausibly describes this same physical line. TransCameron is a standalone 23.4-24-mile Cameron Parish feed-gas lateral serving only the Calcasieu Pass LNG terminal, distinct in route, purpose and ownership (TransCameron Pipeline, LLC / Venture Global) from every other roster entry, including the other Louisiana intrastate/interstate lines (Acadian, Bridgeline, LIG, RIGS, Sea Robin, Creole Trail, Tiger, Kinetica) which serve different corridors and different LNG/market customers. No name or route collision found.

validity.recommendation: flag for Baird review — do not auto-change: verify whether Capacity should be the FERC-certificated maximum (~2,125,000 Dth/d, roughly 2,050-2,125 MMcf/d) rather than the currently staged 1,900.00 MMcf/d
validity.researcher_notes: GEM's current Capacity = 1900.00 MMcf/d. This exact figure IS directly supported by one independent trade-press source: Oil & Gas Journal's Aug. 21, 2019 FID article states 'its 10-million tonne/year Calcasieu Pass LNG plant and associated 1.9-bcfd TransCameron pipeline' (1.9 Bcf/d = 1,900 MMcf/d). HOWEVER, the primary regulatory document — the actual FERC certificate order (166 FERC ¶ 61,144, Feb. 21, 2019, read directly via pdftotext, not via a secondary summary) — states TWICE in its own text that 'TransCameron proposes to construct a new pipeline to provide up to 2,125,000 Dth/d of natural gas transportation service' and 'The project is capable of providing up to 2,125,000 dekatherms per day (Dth/d) of natural gas transportation service.' 2,125,000 Dth/d is materially higher than 1,900 MMcf/d (roughly +8-12% depending on the Btu-to-cf conversion factor used, since 1 Dth ≈ 0.97-1.0 Mcf for typical pipeline-quality gas) — a disagreement between a primary regulator document and a press figure, not something to silently pass per the spec rule. Possible explanations I could not fully resolve within budget: (a) 2,125,000 Dth/d is the certificated maximum design/hydraulic capacity while ~1.9 Bcf/d is the actual firm CONTRACTED capacity under Calcasieu Pass's 100%-of-capacity 20-year precedent agreement (the same order notes 'Calcasieu Pass executed a binding precedent agreement for 100 percent of the firm transportation capacity', so if OGJ's 1.9-bcfd number is quoting the contracted/nameplate throughput rather than the certificate ceiling, both figures could be independently 'true' but describing different things); (b) OGJ's figure is a rounding/press simplification of the FERC number that undershoots it. I did not find a second source stating 2,125,000 Dth/d independent of the FERC order itself (searched EIA, Venture Global's site, NGI, World Oil — none restate the certificated Dth/d figure), nor a second source restating exactly 1,900 MMcf/d independent of OGJ. Recommend Baird decide which figure the Capacity column is meant to record (certificated maximum vs. reported/contracted nameplate) before any change — not staging an edit myself, per the no-auto-apply rule.
